newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway to present 1997 state budget on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Norway to present 1997 state budget on Friday.

text.p: The Norwegian government will present a draft 1997 state budget on Friday with a surplus of an estimated 40 billion crowns ($6.2 billion) thanks to the booming offshore oil and gas industry, analysts said.

The economy is doing so well markets will be looking anxiously for signs of lavish, inflationary spending either in the draft itself or in amendments proposed by parliament before the final budget is adopted in December.
Norway is ruled by a Labour minority government under pressure from the opposition right and left of centre to increase expenditure especially in health care.

Central Bank chief Kjell Storvik last week called for a restrictive fiscal policy and wage moderation in 1997 to keep the country's strong economy under control following higher than expected wage increases last spring.

"Growth in the Norwegian economy is now considerably stronger than among our European trading partners, which makes it more demanding than otherwise to maintain price and wage inflation on a par with our trading partners," Storvik said.
"The risk of further pressures in the economy next year underlines the need for a tight fiscal policy stance in 1997," he said.

Norway, which is the world's largest crude exporter after OPEC giant Saudi Arabia, started running up a budget surplus last year and oil production is expected to remain at more than three million barrels per day for several years to come.
"I think the government will present a tight budget," said Oystein Stephansen, an economist of S-E-Banken, Oslo.

"However, it will show a surplus of perhaps 40 billion crowns. I'm afraid that's going to be an invitation to spend for the parties in the parliament. Therefore we could see a tough struggle in parliament before the final budget is accepted before Christmas."
He expected the surplus in the 1996 budget to approach 50 billion crowns if the oil prices stay on current high levels.
The Finance Ministry, in the revised 1996 budget unveiled in May, projected a surplus of 24.9 billion crowns for this year, but the figure was based on lower oil prices.

The ministry revised upwards its growth projections for overall Gross Domestic Product (GDP) this year to 4.5 percent from initial forecasts of 4.3 percent. The figure for 1997 was put at 2.3 percent.
Mainland GDP, excluding the offshore sector, was set to grow by three percent, up from December 1995 forecasts of 2.7 percent. For 1997, two-percent growth was forecast.
May's forecasts revised down 1996 inflation to 1.25 percent from two percent. Unemployment was expected to continue to fall to an average 4.3 percent in 1996 from 4.9 percent last year.
The central bank, in its third quarterly inflation report issued a week ago, left its projections for inflation unchanged at 1.25 percent for 1996 and 2.5 percent in 1997.
But the bank upgraded estimates for wage growth next year to five percent from second-quarter forecasts of 4.75 percent, while maintaining 1996 growth at 4.25 percent. ($1=6.496 Norwegian Crown)
